question: Choose the sentence with no spelling error.
option_1: I was rently at a literary festival.
option_2: I was recently at a litrary festival.
option_3: I was recently at a literary festival.
option_4: I was recently at a literery fstival.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. I was recently at a literary festival.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The only sentence with no spelling error is "I was recently at a literary festival." — both "recently" and "literary" are spelt correctly here.

• Spelling rule: "Recently" is formed from recent + ly (no letters dropped or transposed); "Literary" (relating to literature) is spelt LITER + ARY, and must not be confused with the similarly spelt but different word "literally".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "I was rently at a literary festival." is incorrect because "rently" is a misspelling of "recently" (the syllable "ce" has been dropped).

• Option 2: "I was recently at a litrary festival." is incorrect because "litrary" is a misspelling of "literary" (the letter "e" after "lit" has been dropped).

• Option 4: "I was recently at a literery fstival." is incorrect because "literery" wrongly replaces the "a" in "literary" with an "e", and "fstival" is a misspelling of "festival" (the letter "e" has been dropped).

NOTE

• Commonly confused/misspelt SSC words: definitely, separate, accommodate, occurrence, embarrass, questionnaire, necessary, privilege.

• Always read each option letter-by-letter against the correctly known spelling rather than skimming, since SSC frequently changes just one letter to create the distractor.

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose 'No improvement' as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.
There has been a noticeable fall in the number of children dying from malnutrition.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. No improvement.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined part "noticeable fall" is already grammatically correct — here "fall" is a noun (meaning a decrease/decline), and a noun must be modified by an adjective, not an adverb.

• Rule: An adjective (e.g., "noticeable") is used to qualify a noun (e.g., "fall"), whereas an adverb (e.g., "noticeably") is used to modify a verb, adjective, or another adverb, never a noun directly.

• Since "fall" functions here as a noun (the complement noun after "has been a"), it correctly takes the adjective "noticeable" before it.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "noticeable falling" is incorrect because it unnecessarily changes the noun "fall" to the gerund "falling", which is not required and disrupts the natural structure "a noticeable fall".

• Option 3: "noticeably falling" is incorrect because it turns "fall" into a present participle modified by an adverb, which no longer fits the structure "There has been a ___" (which requires a noun phrase, not a participle phrase).

• Option 4: "noticeably falls" is incorrect because a finite verb ("falls") cannot follow the article "a" in "There has been a ___"; the blank must be filled by a noun phrase.

NOTE

• Common noun/adverb confusion pairs tested by SSC: a quick increase vs. increasing quickly, a rapid growth vs. growing rapidly, a considerable improvement vs. improving considerably.

• Always check whether the blank is functioning as a noun (needs adjective) or a verb/participle (needs adverb) before choosing the improvement.

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
P. application, which can also be used to log complaints about
Q. littering or caused by the animals, according to officials
R. registered with the local authority through a mobile phone
S. the residents of Noida can now get their pets like dogs or cats
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. SRPQ.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence must begin with S — "the residents of Noida can now get their pets like dogs or cats" — since it is the only part that introduces a complete subject and verb ("the residents ... can get their pets"), while P, Q and R are all incomplete fragments that depend on it.

• S is naturally followed by R — "registered with the local authority through a mobile phone" — because "get their pets ... registered" needs the past participle "registered" immediately after, forming the causative structure "get + object + past participle".

• R is followed by P — "application, which can also be used to log complaints about" — because "mobile phone" must be joined with "application" to form the compound noun "mobile phone application", which the relative clause "which can also be used to log complaints about" then modifies.

• P is followed by Q — "littering or caused by the animals, according to officials" — because "log complaints about" needs its object, "littering or [damage] caused by the animals".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2 (SRPQ).

Additional Information

• Option 1: QRPS is incorrect because it begins with "littering...", a fragment with no clear subject, making the sentence meaningless from the start.

• Option 3: PRQS is incorrect because it begins with "application, which...", but "application" has no antecedent noun ("mobile phone") preceding it yet.

• Option 4: RQPS is incorrect because it begins with "registered with the local authority...", which cannot stand as the opening clause since "registered" requires a preceding subject and the causative verb "get".

NOTE

• In para-jumble questions, first identify the part with a complete, independent subject-verb structure to serve as the starting sentence (here, S).

• Watch for grammatical glue words like "get + object + V3" (causative construction) and compound nouns ("mobile phone application") to link fragments correctly.

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Near 800 million people worldwide lack updated sanitation.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Near 800 million.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the segment "Near 800 million" — the word "Near" is being used incorrectly here; the intended meaning is "almost/approximately", for which the correct word is the adverb "Nearly", not the preposition/adjective "Near".

• Rule: "Near" is normally used as a preposition or adjective of place/time (e.g., "near the station", "in the near future"), while "Nearly" is the adverb used before a number or quantity to mean "almost" (e.g., "nearly 800 million people").

• The corrected sentence should read: "Nearly 800 million people worldwide lack updated sanitation."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "updated sanitation." is not the error — "updated" correctly functions as an adjective modifying "sanitation", and the phrase is grammatically sound.

• Option 2: "people worldwide lack" is not the error — the plural subject "people" correctly takes the plural verb "lack", and "worldwide" is correctly placed as an adverb.

• Option 3: "No error" is incorrect because there is indeed an error, as explained above, in the first segment of the sentence.

NOTE

• Commonly confused word pairs tested by SSC in error-spotting: near/nearly, hard/hardly, late/lately, high/highly, most/mostly.

• Always check whether a word before a number or quantity should be an adverb like "nearly", "approximately", or "almost" rather than a bare adjective/preposition.

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose 'No improvement' as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.
Scientists have predicted that the cultivation of rice will be affected severe.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. affected severely.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined part "affected severe" is incorrect because "affected" is a past participle (part of the passive verb "will be affected"), and a past participle/verb must be modified by an adverb, not an adjective.

• Rule: An adjective (e.g., "severe") modifies a noun, while an adverb (e.g., "severely") modifies a verb, adjective, or another adverb. Since "affected" is a verb form here, it requires the adverb "severely".

• The corrected sentence reads: "Scientists have predicted that the cultivation of rice will be affected severely."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "affect severe" is incorrect because it wrongly changes the verb from "affected" (needed for the passive "will be affected") to the base form "affect", and still retains the adjective "severe" instead of the adverb.

• Option 2: "No improvement" is incorrect because the original phrase "affected severe" is ungrammatical, as an adjective cannot modify a verb.

• Option 3: "effecting severely" is incorrect because "effecting" (from "effect", meaning "to bring about") is the wrong word here; the sentence requires "affected" (from "affect", meaning "to influence"), not "effecting".

NOTE

• Commonly confused pair: affect (verb, to influence) vs. effect (noun, a result; or verb, to bring about).

• Always check whether the blank/underlined word modifies a noun (needs adjective) or a verb (needs adverb) — a very frequently tested SSC error type.

question:
The given sentence is in active voice. Change the voice of the sentence. Select the correct option from the sentences given in options.
She used the aerobic ball during workout.
option_1: During workout the aerobic ball were to be used by her.
option_2: During workout the aerobic ball will be used by her.
option_3: During workout the aerobic ball had been used by her.
option_4: During workout the aerobic ball was used by her.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. During workout the aerobic ball was used by her.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The active sentence "She used the aerobic ball during workout" is in the Simple Past Tense.

• Rule — Simple Past Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + V2 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "the aerobic ball" becomes the subject; being singular, it takes the auxiliary "was"; the verb "used" (V2) becomes the past participle "used" (V3, same form); and "she" becomes the agent "by her".
◦ Passive: The aerobic ball was used by her, during workout.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "were to be used" changes the meaning to an obligation/plan in the past, which is not the Simple Past passive of the given sentence.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "will be used" is the Simple Future passive, not the Simple Past passive required here.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "had been used" is the Past Perfect passive, which wrongly implies the action was completed before another past action.

NOTE

• "Used" is one of many verbs whose V2 and V3 forms are identical (regular verbs); always check the tense of the active sentence carefully before selecting the passive auxiliary.

• Other Simple Past passive examples: "wrote → was written", "made → was made", "bought → was bought".

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.
A child born after the death of his father
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Posthumous.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Posthumous" means occurring, awarded, or born after a person's death (मरणोपरांत). A child described as "posthumous" is one born after the death of his/her father.
◦ Example: The soldier was awarded the medal posthumously, after his death in battle.

• The word comes from Latin postumus, meaning "last" or "last-born", later associated with "post" (after) + "humus" (ground/burial).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Orphan (अनाथ): A child whose parents (one or both) are dead; it does not specifically mean "born after the father's death".

• Option 2: Pseudonym (उपनाम/छद्म नाम): A fictitious name used by an author instead of their real name.

• Option 4: Bigot (कट्टरपंथी): A person who is intolerant of opinions, beliefs, or people different from their own.

NOTE

• Other one-word substitutions related to birth/death often asked in SSC: Widow (a woman whose husband has died), Orphan (a child with no living parents), Posthumous (after death), Nascent (just coming into existence).

question:
Select the option that will improve the bracketed part of the sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement'.
Dad said that, "She would have been a great sister if she was just a bit more careful".
option_2: that, "She would have been a great sister if she were just a bit more careful"
option_3: "She would have been a great sister if she were just a bit more careful"
option_4: "She would have been a greatest sister if she was just a bit more careful"
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. "She would have been a great sister if she were just a bit more careful".

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The bracketed part uses "if she was", which is incorrect because this is a hypothetical/unreal conditional clause, and such clauses require the subjunctive mood "were" for all persons (I/he/she/it), not "was".

• Rule — Subjunctive mood in conditional/hypothetical clauses: In an "if"-clause expressing a wish, supposition, or condition contrary to fact, "were" is used instead of "was" for singular subjects as well (e.g., "If I were you", "if she were").

• The corrected sentence reads: Dad said that, "She would have been a great sister if she were just a bit more careful". Note that the word "that," before the quotation is not part of the bracketed segment being tested and is retained unchanged.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "No improvement" is incorrect because "if she was" is grammatically wrong in this hypothetical clause; it must be "if she were".

• Option 2: 'that, "She would have been a great sister if she were just a bit more careful"' is incorrect because it unnecessarily duplicates the word "that,", which already exists outside the bracketed part in the original sentence, resulting in "that that,".

• Option 4: '"She would have been a greatest sister if she was just a bit more careful"' is incorrect because it wrongly changes "great" to the superlative "greatest" (illogical without a comparison group) and still retains the incorrect "was" instead of "were".

NOTE

• Common subjunctive expressions tested by SSC: "If I were you, I would...", "I wish I were...", "as if/as though she were...", "Suppose he were...".

• The subjunctive "were" is used in unreal/hypothetical conditions, not in real/possible past conditions (e.g., "If she was late, she must have missed the bus" — here "was" is correct because it states a real possibility, not a hypothetical wish).

question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.
Fad
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Sensation.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Fad" means a temporary fashion, craze, or enthusiasm followed keenly for a short time and then dropped (अस्थायी सनक या चलन).
◦ Example: Wearing oversized sunglasses was just a passing fad among teenagers that year.

• "Sensation" is the closest match among the options because it refers to something that creates a widespread, short-lived thrill of public excitement and popularity (सनसनी) — the same sense of a fleeting popular craze that "fad" carries.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Standard (मानक): An accepted level of quality or a measure/rule used as a basis for comparison — opposite in sense to a fleeting fad.

• Option 3: Classic (उत्कृष्ट/चिरस्थायी): Something of recognized, lasting value or quality — the very opposite of something temporary like a fad.

• Option 4: Deviant (विचलित/असामान्य): A person or behaviour that departs from accepted standards; unrelated to the idea of a temporary popular trend.

NOTE

• Words related to "Fad": Craze, Trend, Vogue, Rage, Mania — all denote something popular for a short period.

• Do not confuse "Fad" (temporary popularity) with "Fade" (to lose colour/strength gradually), which is a different word altogether.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
In space it is possible to identify and ________ some unique characteristics of human physiology and biology.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. isolate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct word is "isolate", meaning to separate out and examine something individually/distinctly from the rest (अलग करना).
◦ Example: Scientists were able to identify and isolate the specific gene responsible for the disease.

• The sentence requires a verb parallel to "identify" (joined by "and"), describing what is possible to do with unique characteristics in space — that is, to pick them out and study them separately, which is exactly the sense of "isolate".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: excess (अधिकता): Means "more than necessary/needed"; it does not fit as a verb parallel to "identify" in this context.

• Option 3: replete (परिपूर्ण): Means "filled or well-supplied with something"; grammatically and contextually it does not pair with "identify and ___ some unique characteristics".

• Option 4: partition (विभाजन/बाँटना): Means "to divide into parts"; while it is a verb, dividing is not the same action as identifying and separating out a unique characteristic for study.

NOTE

• "Isolate" is commonly used in scientific/medical contexts: to isolate a virus, isolate a variable, isolate a sample.

• Related word forms: isolation (noun), isolated (adjective) — frequently tested in vocabulary-based fill-in-the-blank questions.

question:
Choose the word that is opposite in meaning to the given word.
Devious
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Outspoken.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Devious" means not straightforward; deceitful, evasive, or willing to lie/cheat to achieve one's aims (कपटी/छलपूर्ण).
◦ Example: He used devious means to win the contract.

• "Outspoken" means direct and open in stating one's opinions, even if they may offend others (स्पष्टवादी) — this is the exact opposite of being sly, evasive, or deceitful, making it the correct antonym.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Circuitous (घुमावदार): Taking a long, indirect route or way of doing something — a synonym of "devious", not its opposite.

• Option 3: Clandestine (गुप्त/गोपनीय): Done secretively, especially because it is illicit — close in meaning to the secretive, underhand sense of "devious".

• Option 4: Serpentine (सर्पिल/टेढ़ा): Winding and twisting like a serpent — literally describes the "roundabout" sense of "devious", hence a synonym, not an antonym.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "devious": shifty, underhand, scheming, crooked, tortuous.

• Other antonyms of "devious": straightforward, honest, candid, direct, forthright.

question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.
Nacreous
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Iridescent.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Nacreous" means resembling mother-of-pearl; having a lustrous, rainbow-like shimmering appearance (सीप जैसी चमकदार).
◦ Example: The nacreous lining of the shell shimmered with different colours in the sunlight.

• "Iridescent" means showing luminous, rainbow-like colours that appear to change when viewed from different angles, which is exactly the same lustrous, shifting-colour quality described by "nacreous", making it the correct synonym.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Monochromatic (एकवर्णी): Having or using only one colour — the opposite of the multi-coloured shimmer of "nacreous".

• Option 2: Pale (फीका/हल्का): Light in colour or lacking intensity — unrelated to the lustrous shimmer of nacreous.

• Option 3: Gloom (उदासी/अंधकार): Darkness or a feeling of sadness — has no connection to the lustrous quality of "nacreous".

NOTE

• "Nacreous" derives from "nacre", another word for mother-of-pearl, the iridescent inner layer of certain mollusc shells.

• Other words describing shimmering/colour-changing surfaces: opalescent, lustrous, pearlescent, shimmering.

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose 'No improvement' as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.
Mary doesn't like cartoons because they are loud, so she doesn't watched them.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. doesn't watch them.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined part "doesn't watched them" is incorrect because the auxiliary "doesn't" (does + not) must always be followed by the base form (V1) of the main verb, never the past tense form.

• Rule: In the Simple Present Tense negative, the structure is Subject + does not/doesn't + V1 (base form) + Object. The auxiliary "does" itself carries the tense/agreement marking, so the main verb stays in its base form.

• The corrected sentence reads: "Mary doesn't like cartoons because they are loud, so she doesn't watch them."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "do not watched this" is incorrect on two counts — it wrongly uses "do" instead of "does" (needed for the singular subject "she"), and it wrongly retains the past form "watched" instead of the base form "watch"; it also wrongly changes "them" to "this".

• Option 3: "No improvement" is incorrect because "doesn't watched them" is ungrammatical, as explained above.

• Option 4: "does watching them" is incorrect because "does" must be followed by the base verb form, not the "-ing" form; "does watching" is not a standard verb structure.

NOTE

• Common error type: mixing an auxiliary (do/does/did) with a wrongly inflected main verb — always ensure only ONE part of the verb phrase carries the tense marking.

• Similarly test: "He doesn't goes" (wrong) → "He doesn't go" (correct); "They didn't went" (wrong) → "They didn't go" (correct).

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.
To play with fire
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. To take foolish risk.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "To play with fire" means to take a foolish or reckless risk; to do something dangerous or engage in a risky activity without regard for the consequences (खतरे से खेलना).
◦ Example: By lying to his business partner, he was playing with fire.

• The idiom draws its imagery directly from the literal danger of handling fire carelessly, which can easily cause harm — hence its figurative use for any reckless, risky behaviour.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Feel sick (बीमार महसूस करना): Simply means to feel unwell; unrelated to risk-taking.

• Option 3: To abuse (दुर्व्यवहार करना): Means to treat someone cruelly or use something improperly; not the meaning of "play with fire".

• Option 4: Show disappointment (निराशा दिखाना): Means to express dissatisfaction or unhappiness; unrelated to the idiom's meaning of risk-taking.

NOTE

• Other idioms of risk/danger often asked in SSC: "To skate on thin ice" (to take a risky course of action), "To live on the edge" (to live dangerously), "To court disaster" (to invite trouble).

question: Choose the incorrectly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Flufy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The incorrectly spelt word is "Flufy"; the correct spelling is "Fluffy" (with a double "f" before the suffix "-y").

• Spelling rule: In many short adjectives formed by adding "-y" to a base word ending in a single consonant after a short vowel, the final consonant is doubled (e.g., "fluff" → "fluffy"), similar to "sun" → "sunny" and "fun" → "funny".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Gifted" is correctly spelt — meaning naturally talented.

• Option 3: "Juggler" is correctly spelt — meaning a person who performs juggling tricks.

• Option 4: "Struggler" is correctly spelt — meaning a person who struggles or strives hard.

NOTE

• Similar doubling-of-consonant spelling patterns tested by SSC: fluffy, muddy, sunny, funny, foggy, shabby.

• Always check for doubled consonants before common suffixes like "-y", "-ed", "-ing" (e.g., "stop" → "stopped", "run" → "running").

question:
Parts of the following sentence are given as options. Identify the part that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.
That was a good / conversation, I look forward / to meet you.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. to meet you.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the segment "to meet you." — the fixed phrase "look forward to" must be followed by a gerund (V-ing form) or a noun, not the base form of the verb.

• Rule: In the expression "look forward to + gerund/noun", the word "to" functions as a preposition, and prepositions in English are always followed by a noun or a gerund, never the base form (infinitive) of a verb.

• The corrected sentence reads: "That was a good conversation, I look forward to meeting you."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "That was a good" is not the error — this segment is grammatically fine as the opening of the sentence.

• Option 3: "conversation, I look forward" is not the error — this segment correctly sets up the fixed expression "look forward to", which is completed (incorrectly) in the next segment.

• Option 4: "No error" is incorrect because there is indeed an error in the segment "to meet you", as explained above.

NOTE

• Other prepositional phrases followed by a gerund often tested by SSC: "look forward to doing", "used to doing" (be accustomed to), "object to doing", "with a view to doing".

• Do not confuse "look forward to + gerund" (a fixed expression) with the infinitive "to + base verb" used after most other verbs (e.g., "I want to meet you").

question:
Select the correct indirect form of the given sentence.
Nandini said, "I bought a pen yesterday."​
option_1: Nandini said she did bought a pen the previous day.
option_2: Nandini said that she had bought a pen the previous day.
option_3: Nandini said that she had bought a pen yesterday.
option_4: Nandini says that she had bought a pen the previous day.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Nandini said that she had bought a pen the previous day.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The direct sentence "I bought a pen yesterday" is in the Simple Past Tense, reported by the verb "said" (past tense, no reporting object).

• Rule — Narration change (Simple Past reported by "said"):
◦ Reporting verb stays "said"; "that" is added before the reported speech.
◦ The pronoun "I" changes according to the subject of the reporting verb → "she".
◦ The tense of the reported verb shifts back one step: Simple Past ("bought") → Past Perfect ("had bought").
◦ The time expression "yesterday" changes to "the previous day".

• Applying the rule: "I bought a pen yesterday" → "she had bought a pen the previous day", giving the full indirect sentence "Nandini said that she had bought a pen the previous day."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Nandini said she did bought a pen the previous day." is incorrect because "did bought" is an ungrammatical double-marking of the past tense; it should simply be "had bought".

• Option 3: "Nandini said that she had bought a pen yesterday." is incorrect because the time expression "yesterday" must change to "the previous day" when reported in indirect speech, since the reporting itself happens at a later, unspecified time.

• Option 4: "Nandini says that she had bought a pen the previous day." is incorrect because the reporting verb has been wrongly changed to the present tense "says", whereas the original reporting verb "said" is in the past tense and must remain "said".

NOTE

• Common time-expression changes in narration: yesterday → the previous day/the day before; today → that day; tomorrow → the next/following day; now → then; here → there; this → that.

• The reporting verb tense is changed only when explicitly changed in the question; if the reporting verb is "said"/"says", it must be reproduced exactly (unless "says"/"will say" allows no backshift of tense).

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Backseat driver
option_1: A person who offers unsolicited advice.
option_3: Attempt to get control over someone.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. A person who offers unsolicited advice.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Backseat driver" means a passenger who constantly gives unwanted or unsolicited advice/instructions to the driver, or more generally, a person who interferes and gives advice on matters that are not their responsibility (बिन मांगी सलाह देने वाला व्यक्ति).
◦ Example: Stop being a backseat driver and let me handle the project my own way.

• The expression comes literally from a passenger sitting in the back seat of a car who keeps telling the driver how to drive, despite not being in control of the vehicle.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: To miss an appointed meeting. is unrelated — this describes failing to attend a scheduled event, not giving unwanted advice.

• Option 3: Attempt to get control over someone. is unrelated — this describes a manipulative or dominating action, not the giving of unsolicited advice.

• Option 4: To conclude proceedings. is unrelated — this simply means to bring something to an end, with no connection to the idiom.

NOTE

• Other idioms about unwanted interference/advice often asked in SSC: "To poke one's nose into" (to interfere in others' affairs), "To put in one's two cents" (to give an opinion, often unasked), "To butt in" (to interrupt or interfere).

question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.
Corrective
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Restorative.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Corrective" means intended to correct, improve, or restore something to its normal or desirable state (सुधारात्मक).
◦ Example: The teacher suggested corrective exercises to improve the student's posture.

• "Restorative" means having the ability to restore health, strength, or a good condition, which closely matches the sense of "correcting/putting right" carried by "corrective", making it the closest synonym.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Commuting (आवागमन करना): Means travelling regularly between one's home and workplace; unrelated to "corrective".

• Option 3: Compensatory (प्रतिपूरक): Means intended to make up for a loss or disadvantage (e.g., compensatory leave); a related but distinct concept from "correcting" a fault.

• Option 4: Sluggish (सुस्त): Means slow-moving or lacking energy; opposite in sense to an active, corrective action.

NOTE

• Related words: correction (noun), correct (verb/adjective), rectify (synonym verb meaning to correct).

• Do not confuse "corrective" (fixing a fault) with "compensatory" (making up for a loss) — SSC often places these as close distractors.

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
Research shows
P. that medium-skilled employees who work
Q. in front of a computer and work beyond
R. 4.6 effective hours a day produce smaller
S. quantities of output per hour due to fatigue
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. PQRS.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The lead-in "Research shows" must be followed by the connector "that", found only at the start of P — "that medium-skilled employees who work" — making P the correct first part.

• P is followed by Q — "in front of a computer and work beyond" — because the relative clause "who work" needs its object/location, "in front of a computer", followed by the parallel verb phrase "and work beyond [some duration]".

• Q is followed by R — "4.6 effective hours a day produce smaller" — because "work beyond" needs a duration to complete its meaning, "4.6 effective hours a day", after which the main verb "produce" appears, needing its object.

• R is followed by S — "quantities of output per hour due to fatigue" — completing "produce smaller" with its object "quantities of output per hour", and giving the reason, "due to fatigue".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4 (PQRS).

Additional Information

• Option 1: RQSP is incorrect because it begins with "4.6 effective hours a day produce smaller...", which has no grammatical subject and cannot follow "Research shows" directly.

• Option 2: PQSR is incorrect because it places S ("quantities of output per hour due to fatigue") directly after Q, before the verb "produce" (in R) has even appeared, making the sentence meaningless.

• Option 3: SQRP is incorrect because it begins with "quantities of output per hour due to fatigue...", which cannot logically follow "Research shows that" as a subject.

NOTE

• In "Research shows that..." type para-jumbles, always locate the part containing the connector "that" to identify the correct opening segment.

• Watch for verb-object pairing (e.g., "produce" needs "smaller quantities of output") and prepositional pairing (e.g., "work beyond [duration]") to sequence the remaining parts correctly.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

Rock candy is actually a collection of large sugar crystals that are "grown" from a sugar-water (1)______. Crystals form when the smallest particles of a substance, the molecules, arrange themselves in a/an (2) ______ and repetitive pattern. Molecules are too small for us to see moving around and (3) ______ themselves, but you can get a rough idea of what this would look like by taking a small shallow tray and filling it with marbles, ball bearings, or other spheres. As you (4) ______ more spheres, the bottom of the tray becomes covered, then the spheres must form layers on top of (5) ______, and a structure or pattern emerges.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. solution.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Blank (1) requires a word describing what a **"sugar-water ___" is, from which sugar crystals are "grown" — this is a "solution"**, i.e., a homogeneous mixture in which sugar (solute) is dissolved in water (solvent).

• Rule/Context: In chemistry, when a solid substance like sugar is dissolved in a liquid like water, the resulting homogeneous mixture is called a solution. Rock candy crystals grow out of a supersaturated sugar-water solution as the water evaporates or cools.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "convergence" means the coming together of different things to a common point; it does not describe a sugar-and-water mixture.

• Option 2: "ramification" means a consequence or complex branching result of an action; it does not fit the context of a sugar-water mixture.

• Option 3: "disposition" means a person's inherent qualities of mind/character, or the arrangement of something; it does not describe a sugar-water mixture.

NOTE

• In cloze passages on scientific topics, look for domain-specific collocations (e.g., "sugar-water solution", "chemical reaction", "molecular structure") rather than general vocabulary.

• Related chemistry terms often tested: solute, solvent, solution, saturation, precipitate, crystallize.

Crystals form when the smallest particles of a substance, the molecules, arrange themselves in a/an (2) ______ and repetitive pattern. Molecules are too small for us to see moving around and (3) ______ themselves, but you can get a rough idea of what this would look like by taking a small shallow tray and filling it with marbles, ball bearings, or other spheres. As you (4) ______ more spheres, the bottom of the tray becomes covered, then the spheres must form layers on top of (5) ______, and a structure or pattern emerges.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. orderly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Blank (2) describes the pattern in which molecules arrange themselves: **"a/an ___ and repetitive pattern". The word "orderly"** (meaning "neat, methodical, following a regular arrangement") pairs naturally with "repetitive" to describe a structured, non-random pattern.

• Rule/Context: The passage explains that crystals form because molecules arrange themselves in a regular, predictable way; "orderly" directly conveys this sense of a systematic, non-chaotic arrangement, contrasted with a random one.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "vastly" means "to a great extent"; it is an adverb of degree and does not fit grammatically or logically as a description of a "pattern" alongside "repetitive".

• Option 3: "wholly" means "entirely, completely"; like "vastly", it is a degree adverb and does not describe the nature of the pattern itself.

• Option 4: "adeptly" means "in a skilful manner"; it describes how an action is performed skilfully, not the nature of a physical/molecular pattern.

NOTE

• Note that the blank requires an adjective (to pair with "and repetitive", also an adjective, both describing "pattern"), which rules out adverbs like "vastly", "wholly", and "adeptly".

• Similar adjective pairs used to describe structured patterns: orderly and systematic, regular and uniform, symmetrical and repetitive.

Rock candy is actually a collection of large sugar crystals that are "grown" from a sugar-water (1)______. Crystals form when the smallest particles of a substance, the molecules, arrange themselves in a/an (2) ______ and repetitive pattern. Molecules are too small for us to see moving around and (3) ______ themselves, but you can get a rough idea of what this would look like by taking a small shallow tray and filling it with marbles, ball bearings, or other spheres. As you (4) ______ more spheres, the bottom of the tray becomes covered, then the spheres must form layers on top of (5) ______, and a structure or pattern emerges.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. arranging.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Blank (3) completes the phrase **"moving around and (3) ___ themselves", describing what molecules do — the correct word is "arranging", which parallels the earlier verb "arrange"** used in the previous sentence ("the molecules, arrange themselves in a/an orderly and repetitive pattern").

• Rule/Context: The two actions joined by "and" — "moving around" and "___ themselves" — must be grammatically and logically parallel; since the molecules are said to "arrange themselves" into a pattern, the parallel ongoing action here is "arranging themselves".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "summarizing" means condensing information into a brief statement; it does not describe a physical action of molecules.

• Option 2: "shielding" means protecting something from harm; unrelated to molecules arranging themselves into a pattern.

• Option 4: "dividing" means splitting into parts; this does not match the sense of molecules coming together to form an orderly pattern.

NOTE

• Cloze passages frequently test the ability to spot a repeated/parallel idea earlier in the passage (here, "arrange themselves" reappears conceptually as "arranging themselves").

• Always re-read the surrounding sentence(s) for repeated key ideas before choosing a blank-filling word in comprehension-based cloze tests.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. add.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Blank (4) completes **"As you (4) ___ more spheres, the bottom of the tray becomes covered" — the correct word is "add"**, meaning to put more spheres into the tray, which logically causes the bottom to gradually become covered.

• Rule/Context: The passage describes a step-by-step demonstration using marbles/ball bearings in a tray; as more spheres are progressively added, they first cover the bottom and then start forming layers on top, which is exactly the cause-and-effect relationship described in the sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "curse" means to invoke harm upon someone/something; it makes no sense in the context of placing spheres in a tray.

• Option 3: "please" means to make someone happy or satisfied; it does not fit the action of putting spheres into a tray.

• Option 4: "toil" means to work hard or labour; it describes effort, not the specific action of putting more spheres into the tray.

NOTE

• Always check that the chosen word logically fits the cause described later in the same sentence (here, "add more spheres" logically causes "the bottom of the tray becomes covered").

• Words related to increasing quantity often tested in cloze passages: add, introduce, insert, supply, accumulate.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

Rock candy is actually a collection of large sugar crystals that are "grown" from a sugar-water (1)______. Crystals form when the smallest particles of a substance, the molecules, arrange themselves in a/an (2) ______ and repetitive pattern. Molecules are too small for us to see moving around and (3) ______ themselves, but you can get a rough idea of what this would look like by taking a small shallow tray and filling it with marbles, ball bearings, or other spheres. As you (4) ______ more spheres, the bottom of the tray becomes covered, then the spheres must form layers on top of (5) ______, and a structure or pattern emerges.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. one another.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Blank (5) completes **"the spheres must form layers on top of (5) ___" — the correct phrase is "one another"**, meaning the spheres form layers stacked on top of each other.

• Rule: "One another" is used to express a reciprocal action or relationship involving more than two entities (here, many spheres), meaning each sphere is on top of some other sphere(s) — exactly the sense required by "layers on top of ___".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "others" is grammatically weak here; "on top of others" is vague and does not carry the precise reciprocal sense of spheres stacking on each other as clearly as "one another" does.

• Option 2: "one" does not fit, since "on top of one" would illogically suggest layering on top of a single specific sphere, rather than describing the general layering process among many spheres.

• Option 4: "every other" means "alternate" (e.g., every other day), which is unrelated to the sense of stacking layers upon each other.

NOTE

• Reciprocal pronoun rule: "Each other" is traditionally used for two entities/people, while "one another" is used for more than two — though in modern usage the two are often used interchangeably.

• Related reciprocal expressions frequently tested by SSC: "look at each other", "help one another", "depend on one another".
